findings.where: First screen, the 'Write to me' margin note (desktop); the same note on phone
findings.fault: The page's only call to action is a small red handwritten scrawl sitting outside the text column, to the left of the margin line, halfway down the screen. It reads as an annotation, not something to click. On desktop the eye goes from the big name heading to the photo and then the aqueduct sketch, and the note is outside that path entirely.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer who has decided to get in touch scans for the way to do it and doesn't find it in the column they are reading. They fall back on the 'Contact' nav link, which is one more step. Mark would object too, because getting in touch is the one thing his homepage is for.

findings.where: First screen, the 'Write to me' link (and the whole page, which has no footer)
findings.fault: The email address is not written out anywhere. The only route to Mark is a mailto link behind the words 'Write to me', so the address stays hidden until a mail program opens.
findings.who_objects: Bank and agency staff on locked-down work machines, where a mailto link often opens nothing or the wrong client. They cannot copy an address they cannot see. First-visit trust item 7 asks for the address in full as its own link text.

findings.where: First screen, the line under the standfirst: 'Over 40 years of international infrastructure experience.'
findings.fault: The one line in the hero set apart in italic is a size claim that can't be checked. It sits right beside a specific, checkable credential (former Lead Lawyer in the World Bank's PPP Group) and weakens it with a brochure-style boast.
findings.who_objects: Procurement-minded staff at development banks, who weigh named roles, bodies and dates and discount year counts as puffery ('Feel the CV': never size words such as '40 years of experience'). Mark asked for confidence without big-firm claims (client value 6).

findings.where: First screen, the heading and standfirst
findings.fault: The 5-second test is only two-thirds met. The hero says who Mark is and what he advises on, but not who he does it for (development banks, agencies, governments) or where (his base, or the regions he works in). 'International' is the only hint.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor from a development agency can't tell at a glance that Mark works for bodies like theirs and in their region. For an advisor, that is the first thing first-visit trust says a visitor must be sure of (items 2 and 6).

findings.where: The whole page, especially next to the call to action
findings.fault: There is no third-party proof. No named body that asked for or published Mark's work appears, and there is no link out to work a bank or agency hosts. The lecture link gives no venue. Apart from the World Bank line, nothing near the action backs it up.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer checking Mark before writing to him finds nothing to verify beyond one job title. First-visit trust item 14 and 'Feel the CV' ask for real, checkable proof (none may be invented).

findings.where: Article page specimen, the large handwritten pull quote 'Whichever PPP Law I am currently working on with a client country!'
findings.fault: The biggest, loudest line in the article is Mark's throwaway joke, set in the handwriting face. Anyone skimming takes the quip as the article's point, while the serious substance ('the elements that make a PPP Law particularly effective') sits in small body text.
findings.who_objects: An agency lawyer skimming the article to judge Mark's thinking finds the flippant line first, which works against the experience-and-judgement voice Mark asked for (brand sheet §5).
